title: What happens to his manuscripts and tapes
summary: Gil explains that manuscripts belong to those he wrote them for, and that he has unheard tapes.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: What is happening to your own tapes and manuscripts?
Are you handling them systematically now? Have you made any......

The manuscripts belong to whoever I wrote the arrangements for you know. So the only manuscripts that I would own would be the ones that I recorded under my own name. And I changed those on the record date sometimes because none of them are really like the record. The only ones that are like the record are the ones I wrote for Miles Davis for example. He owns all those. Some others, I'm not historically minded ( ?).
People like John Lewis for example, with the Modern Jazz Quartet. Now he's got some of the original Capital (secrets?) M

I think John saved those. But I haven't been that way so I really don't have anything like that. I have tapes that I still haven't heard, I want to hear you know. But I went through a phase where I would just walk over to the piano and press on the tape recorder and play something and never hear it again. I've still got some that I've never heard. You know, I'd get a little idea..... It's the wrong thing to do. I did myself a disservice, because when you do a thing like that you should play them over right away.
But I've got all these tapes here and every one so often I get out and eliminate it. You know, I hear it and analyse it and see if I can use that here and I've got a bunch of stuff like that.
